asDecan.p: Your Sun sits between 20 and 29 degrees of Cancer, the last of the sign's three decans, each with its own planet and small card. The Golden Dawn gives this one to the Moon. The Moon also rules Cancer, so here it's at home twice over, running the sign and running your ten degrees of it. That's a slightly odd place for a Sun. The Sun is supposed to be the steady light in a chart, and yours sits in the Moon's own patch, so even your sense of who you are tends to come in phases. The Two of Cups before you is Venus, reaching out to one person. The Three is Mercury, friends with their cups up and everyone talking. Yours is the one that goes quiet, the ripe end of cardinal water, already leaning towards Leo. The Chariot is your Sun card. The Moon's own Major is The High Priestess, the card of knowing things and keeping them to yourself, and there's a lot of her in this slice.

Your weeks have a shape, even if you've never tracked it. There are stretches when you'll say yes to the Friday drinks, the lunch, the cousin's engagement party, and stretches when the phone lighting up on the bench is more than you can face. A message from your mum can sit for two days, and it isn't that you don't care. You're waiting until you've got the room in you to answer it properly. Some evenings you'll pull into the driveway and sit in the car for ten minutes with the engine off before you go in. Nothing's wrong. You just need a gap between the day and the house. When someone asks what you'd like for dinner you honestly might not know, because you've been tuned to what everyone else wanted since eight that morning.

The less obvious gift is that you're hard to sell things to. When a job offer turns up with a bigger salary and everyone around you says take it, you'll sit with it for a week and quite often turn it down, and a year later it's usually clear you read it right. Look at the figure on your card, arms folded, three cups lined up and a fourth being held out from a cloud. Most people see boredom there. I tend to see someone who knows what they've already got and isn't about to grab at the next thing because it's shiny. You're also good on your own, which plenty of people aren't. You can see a film by yourself on a Tuesday night, or eat at the bar with a book, and that's often the best night of your week.

The harder thing is the decisions you make on a low day. With the Moon this strong your mood does drop, and when it does, the job, the flat and sometimes the partner all start to look like the problem. You can draft a resignation letter on a grey Thursday that you'd never have written on a good Monday. Then there are the invitations. You say no to the barbecue, then the weekend away, then a birthday, each for a decent reason, and after the third time people stop asking. Then you feel left out, and a bit hurt, though nobody did anything wrong. Some of that is Cancer wanting to be chased a little. It's worth knowing that about yourself, because most friends won't think to do the chasing.

When something goes badly, a breakup, a redundancy, a death in the family, you go quiet before you do anything else. The first few days show up in the body. You sleep ten hours or four, you forget to eat or live on toast at odd times, and you tell people you're fine in a voice that closes the subject. A week later you're often still in, but now you're going over it, replaying old conversations, sometimes ones from years back, trying to find where it went wrong. A partner who wanted to help and wasn't allowed can feel very shut out. With the Moon running this decan, what helps is rhythm. Small meals at proper times, up at the same hour, curtains open by nine. Someone who drops food round and doesn't need to talk. Then, after a few days, one honest phone call to the person you've been avoiding.

A good evening with someone you love might be the two of you in the same room, each with a book or a show, hardly talking, and that counts as closeness to you. A partner who needs to chat the whole way through dinner, or who reads your quiet as a sulk, can wear you down without either of you knowing why. The quiet does turn into a sulk sometimes, though, and that's the part to watch. When you're hurt you tend to go silent and wait to see if they notice. Plenty of decent partners don't, because they simply can't read the signal, and you end up feeling unloved by someone who loves you a great deal. It helps to say it in words, even clumsily. "I'm upset about Saturday and I need you to ask me about it" is enough.

Work tends to go well for you when it means looking after something over a long stretch. Nursing, teaching, hospitality, a family business, an archive, anything with a long memory. You'd sooner keep one client for ten years than chase a new one every week, and you're very good at picking up what a customer or a team needs before they've said it. Your energy runs in cycles, though, and a job that wants the same numbers from you every week grinds you down. Where you can, save the heavy work for the weeks you've got energy and keep the flat weeks for admin. And look at what's already being offered, the side project, the transfer, the course your manager has mentioned twice. With this decan the next good thing is usually on the table somewhere, and you've probably walked past it more than once.

At twenty this slice of Cancer is often quite hard on itself. You feel a lot and assume everyone else is coping better, and there can be a stretch of staying in your room, turning down things you later wish you'd gone to. By the mid-thirties most people with this decan have learnt their own rhythm. They know the low weeks come and go, they stop making big decisions inside them, and they've usually built a home that works as a proper place to recover. The Leo next door starts to show a bit too, some warmth in company, a bit less hiding. The fifties tend to bring an ease with it all, and a lot of late Cancers I've seen start saying yes to things they'd have turned down at thirty. The trip with the cousins, the pottery class, a second go at love after a long gap.

Keep a short list on your phone called 'offered'. Each time someone holds something out to you, an invitation, a compliment, help with the move, a lead on a job, write it down in a few words, whether you took it or not. Once a month, on the full moon if you like that sort of thing, read back through it. Pick one thing you let pass and go back to the person about it. Ask if it still stands, or just thank them properly.
